scene: You part on a path and point back to the same spot, to meet there again soon.
root: até possibly Arabic ḥattā ‘until’ (disputed); logo ← Latin locō ‘on the spot’
definition_pt: O que se diz quando vai embora e espera ver a pessoa de novo.
parts_meaning: até = "until, up to; even"; logo < Latin locō "in the place"
cognates: Spanish hasta luego (luego = logo)
culture: Até logo is a friendly, neutral goodbye and doesn't have to mean the same day. | The most common casual Brazilian goodbye is tchau, from Italian ciao, which comes from Venetian s-ciao "(I am your) slave," originally a deferential greeting, from Latin sclavus.

scene: Darkness settles; a quiet greeting as the sky goes black.
definition_pt: O que se diz para cumprimentar ou para ir embora, à noite.
pt_family: bom dia (good morning) | boa tarde (good afternoon)
culture: Unlike English, one phrase covers both "good evening" (arriving at 8 pm dinner) and "good night" (leaving or going to bed). Switch from boa tarde at dusk.

scene: The sun hangs lower, the air slows; you greet someone in the late light.
definition_pt: O que se diz para cumprimentar depois do almoço, até a noite.
parts_meaning: boa < Latin bona; tarde < Latin tardē "late, slowly"
origin: bona → boa (intervocalic n dropped); see bom and tarde.
cognates: Spanish buenas tardes
pt_family: bom dia (good morning) | boa noite (good evening)

scene: Morning light floods the sky; you greet someone under the brightness.
root: Latin bonum + diēs ‘day’ (from a root ‘to shine’)
definition_pt: O que se diz para cumprimentar de manhã, até o almoço.
parts_meaning: bom < Latin bonum; dia < Latin diēs "day"
origin: bonum → bom (final -n became a nasal vowel); feminine boa < bona (intervocalic n dropped). Latin diēs → Vulgar Latin dia.
cognates: Spanish buenos días | French bonjour and Italian buongiorno (both use diurnum for "day")
pt_family: boa tarde (good afternoon) | boa noite (good evening)
culture: greetings by time of day | Bom dia: from waking up until about noon or lunch. | Boa tarde: from noon until dusk (roughly 6 pm). | Boa noite: after dark, both as "good evening" when arriving and "good night" when leaving. | Brazilians greet a room, a shop, or an elevator with these. Walking into a store without a bom dia can seem a bit cold.

scene: You pause in a doorway and wait for a nod before stepping through.
definition_pt: O que se diz, com educação, antes de passar, entrar ou interromper.
parts_meaning: cum = "with"; licentia = "freedom, permission," from licēre "to be allowed" + -entia (abstract noun "-ence")
origin: Two Latin words kept together: cum (see com) + licentia (see licença).
history: Why English split: For the polite phrase, English says excuse me, from Latin ex + causa ("out of the charge/accusation"). English asks to be let off the blame, often after the fact. Portuguese asks for permission before acting.
cognates: Spanish con licencia | Italian con licenza
pt_family: desculpa (sorry, after the fact)
synonyms: licença | dá licença | com sua licença
culture: It's literally a request for a license to act: to get past someone, step into a room or someone's home, interrupt, leave the table, or take something. | It's said before the action. Desculpa / desculpe ("sorry") is said after you bump into someone or make a mistake. | Common replies: Pois não ("of course / go ahead"), Fique à vontade ("make yourself comfortable"). A playful Brazilian reply is Toda! ("all of it," meaning you have all the permission you need). That one is informal.

english: how are you? (formal, to a woman)
scene: The elder woman walks in; you watch how her steps are going, and the room makes space.
root: Latin quōmodo + vādere + feminine of seniōrem
definition_pt: Pergunta educada para uma mulher, quase sempre mais velha: como ela está.
literal: a respectful greeting to a woman, especially an older one
parts_meaning: "how goes the lady?"
origin: see components.
cognates: Spanish ¿Cómo está usted, señora?
pt_family: como vai o senhor? | como vai você?

english: how are you? (formal, to a man)
scene: The white-haired elder walks in; you watch how his steps are going, and the room makes space.
definition_pt: Pergunta educada para um homem, quase sempre mais velho: como ele está.
literal: the respectful version of como vai?. The verb stays 3rd person because you're grammatically talking about "the gentleman."
parts_meaning: "how goes the gentleman?"
origin: see components.
cognates: Spanish ¿Cómo está usted?
pt_family: como vai a senhora? | como vai você?
culture: Use it with an older man, a hotel manager, a client.

scene: You watch the other person's stride, still from a slight formal distance.
definition_pt: Pergunta normal, não formal: como a outra pessoa está.
literal: a friendly como vai?. Answer: Vou bem, e você?
parts_meaning: "how goes you (Your Grace)?"
origin: see components.
cognates: French Comment vas-tu?
pt_family: como vai o senhor? | como vai a senhora?

scene: Someone walks toward you; you watch the pace and the set of their shoulders.
definition_pt: Pergunta comum quando encontra alguém: como a pessoa está.
parts_meaning: "how goes (it)?"
origin: see como and vai.
cognates: French Comment ça va? | Spanish ¿Cómo te va? | Italian Come va? | German Wie geht's? | old English How goes it?
pt_family: como vai você? (how are you?, informal)
synonyms: tudo bem? | como está? | e aí? (casual)
culture: It's a bit more polite or classic than Tudo bem?. Typical answer: Vou bem, obrigado, e você? ("I go well, thanks, and you?") or just Bem, obrigado.

scene: Stepping away from a vast harbor city of towers.
root: Latin dē + nova + York (Old English Eoforwīc ← Latin Eboracum ← Celtic, probably ‘place of yews’)
definition_pt: Que vem da cidade de Nova York.

scene: You turn and look back down the road, to the place someone came from.
definition_pt: Pergunta o lugar de origem: “De onde você é?”
parts_meaning: onde < Latin unde "from where, whence"
origin: Latin unde meant "from where," but in Portuguese onde drifted to plain "where." So Portuguese added de again: de onde is historically "from from-where." Spanish donde is itself de + unde fused, which makes ¿de dónde? a double-double.
history: Why English split: English has its own whence (Germanic), but it's archaic, so English says "from where." Portuguese onde lost its "from" meaning, so it needed de again.
cognates: Spanish ¿de dónde?
notes: De onde você é? = "Where are you from?" Also aonde = "to where" (a + onde).

scene: Almost nothing in the palm — far too little.
root_image: est = it is; multum here is "very," turning the smallness up; paucum = little, a pinch. The amount is not just small — it is very small.
definition_pt: É uma quantidade muito pequena.
parts_meaning: é < est; muito here is the adverb "very"; pouco < Latin paucum "few, little" (already in um pouco)
origin: pouco < paucum (au → ou). muito before an adjective or adverb means "very" (muito pouco, muito bem, muito gentil). So é muito pouco is stronger than é pouco: it's very little.
cognates: Spanish es muy poco | Italian è molto poco | French c'est très peu
pt_family: um pouco (a little) | não é muito (it's not much)
notes: muito here means "very," not "a lot of": muito pouco = very little.

scene: A nod, shoulders settling — everything stands all right where it is.
root_image: stāre = to stand, to be in a place or state right now; bene = well. The situation stands well — it is all right.
definition_pt: Tudo está certo, sem problema. Também: “ok.”
parts_meaning: está < Latin stat, from stāre "to stand"; bem < Latin bene "well"
origin: The same estar < stāre already in onde está?, plus bem < bene (already in bem, muito bem, tudo bem). Together they mean the state is good: está bem = "it's okay / all right." In speech está often shortens to tá: tá bem.
history: English link: English stand is the Germanic cousin of stāre; well is Germanic too. English okay / all right covers the same job. Portuguese describes the state as standing well.
cognates: Spanish está bien | Italian sta bene | French ça va / c'est bien | English stand, stable; bene- (benefit, benediction)
pt_family: estar (to be, for now) | tudo bem (all good) | muito bem (very well) | tá bem (casual)
notes: In speech, está is often tá: Tá bem. Close in meaning to tudo bem, but está bem can also answer a request: "Is that all right?" — Está bem.

scene: You taste and find nothing — a slow shake of the head, empty hands.
definition_pt: O que eu digo quando a resposta não está na minha cabeça.
parts_meaning: eu < Latin ego; não < Latin nōn "not"; sei is the irregular 1st-person present of saber, "to know"
origin: Latin nōn became Portuguese não (the tilde marks a nasal vowel). sei belongs to saber, from Latin sapere "to taste, to have flavor." That physical sense developed a mental one: to have discernment, to be wise, to know. The 1st-person present is irregular: eu sei, not *sabo (compare Spanish sé, French sais, Italian so).
pt_family: quem sabe (who knows; maybe)

scene: You point into the distance, to a spot already fixed in place, over there.
root: fīgere ‘to fix’ + Latin illāc ‘that way, over there’
definition_pt: Está naquele lugar, longe de nós: “O hotel fica lá.”
pt_family: onde fica? (where is it?)

scene: A teacher's hands open wide, a deep nod, again and again.
definition_pt: Bem de verdade. Também se diz para elogiar: “Muito bem!”
parts_meaning: see muito and bem
origin: Latin multum bene.
cognates: Spanish muy bien | Italian molto bene | French très bien
notes: It's also praise, "Well done!", the way a teacher would say it. Estou muito bem = "I'm very well."

scene: The binding cord of thanks pulled tighter, a deeper bow.
root_image: The same binding as obrigado: a cord looping around the wrist, tying you to the person who helped you — pulled tighter this time, with more of you in the knot.
definition_pt: Obrigado, com mais força: o que um homem diz quando alguém é muito gentil.
parts: muito (very, much) + obrigado (obliged, thank you — said by a man)
parts_meaning: muito < multum "much, very"; obrigado < Latin obligātus "bound, obliged" (ob- + ligāre "to bind")
origin: The everyday obrigado / obrigada of Lesson 2, intensified with muito. A man says muito obrigado; a woman says muito obrigada. The phrase is the Portuguese equivalent of English much obliged, and it is built of the same Latin pieces (multum + obligātus), even though everyday English now prefers thank you very much.
history: English link: much obliged is the exact English cousin, now a bit old-fashioned; thank you very much uses Germanic thank. The Latin pieces are still visible in obliged / obligation. Portuguese just says the everyday words: muito obrigado.
cognates: English much obliged, obliged, obligation | Spanish muy obligado (rare; usually muchas gracias) | Italian molto obbligato | French très obligé
pt_family: obrigada (thank you, said by a woman) | obrigar (to oblige, to force)
notes: Said by a man. A woman says muito obrigada. Replies: de nada, por nada, imagina, não há de quê.

scene: A warm, easy smile spreading as you meet someone, like a pleasant taste.
definition_pt: O que se diz quando conhece uma pessoa pela primeira vez.
parts: muito (much) + praz- (please) + -er (infinitive, used as a noun)
pt_family: o prazer é meu (the pleasure is mine) | igualmente (likewise)
culture: Said when you're introduced. Replies: O prazer é meu ("the pleasure is mine") or Igualmente ("likewise"). | It often comes with a handshake. In social settings Brazilians, especially women, greet with cheek kisses; the number varies by region and person (often one in São Paulo, two in Rio), so follow the other person's lead. | Just Prazer! works casually.

scene: A thick sheaf of dollar notes filling the hands.
root_image: multus = many, a packed crowd; the dollar's name is the Thaler, a coin from Joachim's Valley, now in a thick stack.
definition_pt: Uma grande quantidade de dólares.
parts_meaning: muitos is the masculine plural of muito < Latin multum; dólares is the plural of dólar, from German Thaler
origin: muito agrees in number and gender: muito (adv.), muita, muitos, muitas. With dólares (masculine plural) it is muitos dólares. The noun dólar is the same Thaler / Joachimsthaler borrowing as in Lesson 5.
history: English link: many is Germanic; multi- keeps the Latin root. dollar and dólar are the same Thaler word.
cognates: English many dollars (Germanic many + the same dollar) | Spanish muchos dólares | Italian molti dollari
pt_family: muito (much, very) | muitas (many, fem.) | dólar / dólares | muitos reais
notes: muitos agrees with dólares (masc. pl.). Feminine would be muitas.

scene: Fingers opening a wallet; the money is inside it, in their fold.
root_image: in = in, inside; a + sua mark the wallet as hers/yours; the wallet itself is the paper-holder. The whole picture is: inside the fold that belongs to the other person.
definition_pt: Dentro da carteira de você.
parts: na (in the, fem.) + sua (your, fem.) + carteira (wallet)
parts_meaning: na = em + a (in + the, feminine); sua = your (fem.); carteira = wallet
origin: na is the regular contraction of em + a, the same pattern as no = em + o. sua agrees with carteira (feminine). The three pieces fuse into one everyday phrase: na sua carteira.
cognates: Spanish en tu cartera / en su cartera | Italian nella tua cartella (different noun) | French dans ton portefeuille
pt_family: sua carteira (your wallet) | na minha carteira (in my wallet)
notes: na = em + a. With a masculine noun it would be no (no hotel). sua agrees with carteira.

scene: Looking at a small amount and shaking the head: that isn't a lot.
root_image: nōn = not; est = it is; multum = much. The amount standing in front of you is not a large one.
definition_pt: Não é uma quantidade grande.
parts_meaning: não < nōn; é < Latin est "is"; muito < multum
origin: A whole-clause version of não muito: é (from Latin est, already in Lesson 1) sits in the middle, so the phrase is a full sentence, "it is not much."
history: English link: English is and much are both Germanic. The Latin pieces survived as non- and multi-; Portuguese just says the everyday words in a line: não é muito.
cognates: Spanish no es mucho | Italian non è molto | French ce n'est pas beaucoup
pt_family: não muito (not much) | é muito pouco (it's very little)

scene: A small shake of the head over a short pile — not a lot.
root_image: Latin nōn = not; multum = much, many. Together: not a large amount.
definition_pt: Uma quantidade pequena: não é uma quantidade grande.
parts_meaning: não < Latin nōn "not"; muito < Latin multum "much, many"
origin: The same nōn → não and multum → muito already in earlier lessons, now joined: não muito.
history: English link: English much is Germanic (Old English micel). The Latin multum survived in English as multi-, multiply, multitude. Portuguese keeps one everyday word, muito, and negates it with não.
cognates: English multi-, multiply, multitude | Spanish no mucho | Italian non molto | French pas beaucoup (different words)
pt_family: muitos (many) | não é muito (it's not much) | pouco (little)
notes: Não muito answers a question about amount: Você sabe português? — Não muito.

scene: Inside the guest-house, within its walls.
root: Latin in + illum + French hôtel ← Latin hospitāle
root_image: in + o = in the; the hotel is the guest-house (hospitāle). The picture is being inside that house, not just looking at it from the street.
definition_pt: Dentro do hotel, ou no hotel.
parts_meaning: no = em + o (in + the, masculine); hotel from French hôtel ← Latin hospitāle (guesthouse)
cognates: Spanish en el hotel (no contraction) | Italian in albergo / nell'hotel | French à l'hôtel | English in the hotel, at the hotel
pt_family: o hotel (the hotel) | no restaurante (at/in the restaurant)
notes: no = em + o. Use na before a feminine noun (na carteira, na mala). The h of hotel is silent: no-o-TÉL.

scene: You scan the room for something upright in its spot, right now.
definition_pt: Pergunta o lugar de alguém ou de alguma coisa agora: “Onde está a mala?”
literal: "where does it stand?" = where is it (right now)?
origin: unde → onde; stat → está (see onde and estar).
pt_family: onde fica? (where is it located?)

scene: You look for the place a stake was driven — fixed, unmoving.
root: Latin unde + fīgere ‘to fix, fasten’ (via reconstructed *figicāre)
definition_pt: Pergunta o lugar fixo de alguma coisa: “Onde fica o hotel?”
literal: "where is it fixed?", which is why it's used for buildings, cities, and things that don't move
pt_family: fica lá (it's over there)
notes: Used for places and other fixed locations.

scene: An open hand, offered with warmth, asking a kindness in return.
definition_pt: Palavras educadas para pedir alguma coisa.
parts_meaning: por < Latin pro "for, on behalf of" (blended with per "through"); favor < Latin favor "goodwill, support," from favēre "to be well-disposed"
origin: both words came straight from Latin with little change.
history: Why English split: English kept favor almost unchanged, but its polite word is please, short for "if you please," from Latin placēre (the same root as prazer). English says "if it pleases you"; Portuguese says "as a favor."
cognates: Spanish por favor | Italian per favore
notes: Formal signs and polite requests also use por gentileza (see gentil). Faz favor is more typical of Portugal.

scene: The whole scene is at ease — nothing out of place.
definition_pt: Pergunta e resposta do dia a dia: “Tudo bem?” “Tudo bem!” Também quer dizer “sem problema”.
cognates: Spanish todo bien | Italian tutto bene | French tout va bien
culture: Tudo bem? is the default Brazilian greeting, and Tudo bem is the default answer. Tudo bem? — Tudo bem, e você? Like "How's it going? — Good, you?", it's a ritual, not a real health check. | Variants: Tudo bom? — Tudo ótimo!, Tudo certo?, E aí, tudo bem? ("Hey, all good?"), the casual Beleza? ("Beauty?" = "Cool?"). | It also means "It's OK / no problem" after an apology: Desculpa! — Tudo bem. | It often comes with a thumbs up, which Brazilians call joia ("jewel").

scene: A pinch held between two fingers — just that much.
definition_pt: Uma quantidade pequena: não muito.
parts_meaning: um < Latin unum "one"; pouco < Latin paucum "few, little"
origin: unum → um (the n became nasalization); paucum → pouco (au → ou, a regular change).
cognates: English one, unit, unique (unus) | Spanish un poco | Italian un poco | French un peu
notes: Falo um pouco de português = "I speak a little Portuguese." Brazilians love the diminutive um pouquinho ("a tiny bit").
